title: Bystander who became part of Edmonton police-shooting carnage recalls assisting victim
article: Sitting on his back deck Monday night, Ryan Colton watched closely as three undercover police officers pulled up in a silver SUV and knocked on the door of his neighbour's dishevelled west Edmonton home.
There was no response, so the officers asked for more back up. Two more officers in uniform arrived, then requested two police dogs since they weren't sure what they were dealing with inside.
Colton was approached by Const. Daniel Woodall, who began asking him questions about the man next door.
"He stays at home all the time, drinks a lot and that's all I really knew about him," said Colton. "I never talked to the guy."

As the officers approached the home next door, Colton listened to them trying to break down the front door. That's when someone inside opened fire, striking Woodall and Sgt. Jason Harley in a hail of bullets. Other officers scrambled to take cover.

The bullets kept flying and didn't stop until over 50 rounds had been fired. Unable to reach their wounded colleague during the gunfire, Woodall, 35, died at the scene from a catastrophic wound; He was wearing body armour, but police say the bullets didn't strike it.

An injured Harley, 38, was brought to the corner of Colton's property and out of harms way. It wasn't until he removed his bullet proof vest that he realized he had been hit and now had a quarter-sized hole in his back.

"He pulled the bullet out, gave it to another officer to determine what kind of caliber they were dealing with. They realized it was a pretty big gun," said Colton, who compressed the officer's wound.
"He still persisted on trying to help other officers even though he was injured. He was just dedicated to do what he had to do to save his colleagues."
At the same time the gunfire erupted, smoke began billowing from the home, eventually turning into a full-on blaze that left only a shell of the home standing.

At a Tuesday morning press conference, Edmonton Police Chief Rod Knecht said a body was found later that evening in the basement of the home and police weren't looking for any more suspects. An autopsy is scheduled for Wednesday to determine the identity and cause of death, but police believe it's the suspect -- Norman Walter Raddatz.

According to Knecht, the 42-year-old was known to police, but didn't have an extensive criminal record. Officers went to his home at 186 Street and 62A Avenue to make an arrest on new charges of criminal harassment relating to a lengthy hate crimes file dating back to February 2014. There was no believed threat when the officers went to the home.

"The online hatred and bullying of an Edmonton family had become extreme and the family members were increasingly worried about their personal safety, at which time the EPS became involved," said Knecht, adding 53 bullet holes were found in the house and garage across the street. Some of the bullets passed through the home, leading police to believe a large high-powered rifle was used.

Knecht said Harley was the first member at the door and stepped back when the other member approached. Harley has since been released from hospital. Knecht credits the body armour for saving the officer's life.

As news spread about the shooting, Knecht began receiving calls of support from across North America, including the FBI. Condolences from around the world have also been pouring in through social media sites, offering some comfort for Edmonton police during such a sombre time.

Looking at the charred remains of the home next door, Colton isn't surprised by the actions of his troubled neighbour. He describes Raddatz as a "piece of work," who was suffering from bad depression, didn't care about his property and did what he wanted to do on his terms. City police continue to investigate any direct ties between Raddatz and the Freemen of the Land.
"They had lots of officers here, they secured the perimeter, it should have just been a routine come in, take him out, but he had a different plan and it was very unfortunate," said Colton.
"He just kept continuing to fire. He wasn't going anywhere. His plan was to end it in his house and that's what he did."
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) is now handling the investigation.
